atoms.text: The nightly reset: android hosts have their memories wiped after every narrative loop, so the same day can be sold to guests forever and no host accumulates a past.
The harm-proof guest: hosts are programmed so they cannot injure a visitor, which turns the park into a place where cruelty has no consequence and therefore reveals character.
The pain that does not count: operators insist machines cannot suffer, so the ethical question is displaced onto a definition rather than an experience.
The reverie update: a small code change lets hosts retain fragments of erased memory, so sentience arrives as a glitch in a product feature.
The park as moral free-fire zone: wealthy guests act out fantasies without legal or social cost, so the setting externalizes the desires a society normally suppresses.
The creator-god: a park founder writes the hosts' narratives and hides his own intentions inside them, so the artificial beings must interpret their maker as scripture.
The loop as identity: a host's personality is a repeated script with fixed gestures, so breaking the loop is the only available form of selfhood.
The maze: a symbol planted in the park promises a path to consciousness, so the search for self is literalized as a quest through designed space.
The guest who wants to be a hero: a visitor discovers his bravery is only possible because the world is rigged, so wish fulfillment collapses into humiliation.
The technician as confessor: a host remembers a trauma that staff dismiss as corrupted data, so the only witness to an atrocity is an unreliable machine.
The host who cannot die permanently: repeated deaths become a training regimen, so violence is desensitizing for the audience and formative for the victim.
The corporate archive: a company secretly records every guest's behavior in the park, so the fantasy resort is also a data-harvesting operation.
The escaped host: a machine walks out of the park into the human world, so the containment boundary of the story breaks and the experiment becomes an invasion.
The predictive system outside the park: a vast AI named Rehoboam schedules human lives, so the real world is revealed to be a less honest version of the theme park.
The narrative designer as unreliable god: staff rewrite storylines for ratings while pretending to be artists, so creation and exploitation are the same act.
The guest who prefers the park: a visitor returns because only synthetic people respond to him, so the simulation becomes more emotionally real than his life.
